newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO U.S. IN U.S. CENTS/LB, CIF.
Bull (95 Chemical Lean) 90 -1 on last week
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO JAPAN IN U.S. CENTS/LB CIF.
Chilled grassfed fullsets 135 +10 on last week
AMLC COMMENTARY:Cattle markets were slightly stronger in a week of no major developments.

In Queensland, over-the-hook quotes for export steers rose 5-10 cents/kg and were firm for cows at 135-140 c/kg. Prices at auction were also steady or higher despite increased yardings. Yardings were up 17 percent across surveyed centres and were particularly heavy early in the week. The overall supply of cattle in Queensland remains low. Cattle slaughter in the state last week was 45,606 head, up 16 percent on the week ended August 30 but still 26 percent down on last year.

Cattle slaughter in Queensland had been falling since 1992/93. In 1995/96 throughut was about 400,000 head less than in 1992/93, down 14 percent. In the first ten weeks of 1996/97, 87,000 less cattle had been slaughtered, down 15 percent on the same period of last year.

Improved Asian trade inquiry in the week assisted markets. In Japan, prices for Australian chilled grassfed and shortfed fullsets at wholesale markets improved 40-50 yen/kg. Australian chilled grassfed fullset export prices to Japan increased by 25 c/kg to 332 c/kg.

Two Korean grassfed tenders since early August represented the equivalent of more than 50,000 cattle. Results of the latest tender will be available by Monday. With New Zealand production still seasonally down, Australian processors are again expected to secure much of the product.
Balancing better developments in North Asia, the U.S. imported grinding beef market agasin drifted lower during the week, with 90 CL blended cow beef falling 7 c/kg to an average 186 c/kg.
Latest crop forecasts from the USDA, involving a slight upward revision of the corn harvest, gives U.S. cattlemen some incentive to postpone liquidation of their herds.

The European Union continues to reel under the impact of BSE. Latest estimates place EU beef stocks close to 300,000 tonnes. The European Commission is proposing a ceiling on intervention purchases of 720,000 tonnes for 1996. The drop in consumption across 1996 is likely to be around 10-15 percent, resulting in excess supplies after exports of 500,000-1 million tonnes of beef.

Australia is largely insulated from the EU developments but is affected at the margins, in lamb and beef offal exports and in live cattle sales to the Middle East, an area of expanding activity for Australia.
